metadata.title: Understanding the relationship between teacher collaboration beliefs and job satisfaction via collaborative attitudes: A moderated mediation model of classroom self-efficacy from PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 teacher questionnaires with a cross-nationally representative sampling design, where schools were selected and about 20 teachers were randomly sampled per school. The analytic sample is restricted to well-matched teachers and schools with complete questionnaire responses for the constructs used. The manuscript does not report applying PISA teacher sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure; therefore, the weighting strategy is not documented for this analysis. For analysts replicating the work with PISA 2022 teacher microdata, the recommended approach is to use the official PISA teacher/sampling weights provided in the dataset (and replicate weights if available) to account for the complex sampling and clustering by school.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are generated for student cognitive achievement domains in PISA, but this study models teacher collaboration beliefs, collaborative attitudes, job satisfaction, and classroom self-efficacy as latent constructs from teacher questionnaire items. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. Missing data handling is reported as pairwise deletion, so the missing-data strategy is documented for the included variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample includes only the well-matched 40,349 teachers and schools from the PISA 2022 teachers’ questionnaires. Missing values were cleaned using pairwise deletion: only non-missing pairs of variables were included in the analyses, with excluded missingness ranging from 4.45% (teacher collaborative attitudes) to 21.22% (teachers collaboration beliefs). The study uses teacher questionnaire latent constructs (collaboration beliefs, collaborative attitudes, job satisfaction, classroom self-efficacy) and additionally performs moderation/subgroup analyses by teacher gender, while controlling teacher background variables and school-level SES.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural equation model (standardized effect): β = 0.162, p < 0.001; 95% CI [0.153, 0.170].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Teacher collaboration beliefs to predict Teacher collaborative attitudes, finding that collaboration beliefs had a positive direct association (β = 0.162, p < 0.001). This indicates that strengthening teachers’ beliefs in trust and collaboration is likely to support more frequent collaborative attitudes in schools, although the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Direct effect of collaboration beliefs on job satisfaction: β = 0.002, p > 0.646 (95% CI [-0.006, 0.011]); direct effect of collaborative attitudes on job satisfaction: β = 0.073, p < 0.001 (95% CI [0.062, 0.083]); indirect effect (collaboration beliefs → collaborative attitudes → job satisfaction): β = 0.012, p < 0.001 (95% CI [0.010, 0.014]); total effect: 0.848 (as reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Teacher collaboration beliefs and Teacher collaborative attitudes to predict Teacher job satisfaction, finding no significant direct link from collaboration beliefs to job satisfaction (β = 0.002, p > 0.646) but a significant positive indirect pathway through collaborative attitudes (β = 0.012, p < 0.001) and a significant direct effect of collaborative attitudes on job satisfaction (β = 0.073, p < 0.001). This indicates that policy and school leadership should focus on translating collaboration beliefs into collaborative attitudes to improve teacher well-being, while recognizing that cross-sectional SEM results cannot confirm causality.

main_findings.target_variable: Moderated mediation pathways to Teacher job satisfaction
main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderation of direct effect (collaboration beliefs × classroom self-efficacy): β = 0.750, p < 0.001; moderation of indirect effect (collaborative attitudes × classroom self-efficacy): β = −0.082, p < 0.001; gender moderation: collaboration beliefs × female β = 0.746, p < 0.001; collaboration beliefs × male β = 0.146, p < 0.001; collaborative attitudes × female β = 0.068, p < 0.001; collaborative attitudes × male β = 0.014, p = 0.013.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Classroom self-efficacy and Teacher gender to predict the strength of the collaboration-beliefs-to-job-satisfaction pathways, finding that classroom self-efficacy significantly amplified the direct effect (β = 0.750, p < 0.001) while weakening the indirect effect through collaborative attitudes (β = −0.082, p < 0.001), and that the collaboration-beliefs association with job satisfaction was stronger for female teachers than male teachers. This indicates that interventions to improve teacher job satisfaction should be gender-responsive and should build classroom self-efficacy, because the effectiveness of collaboration-related mechanisms depends on these conditions.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data from 40,349 teachers and schools across 17 countries/economies (including ARE, PRT, DEU, KOR, and others). The analysis is a moderated mediation framework: teacher collaboration beliefs predict teacher collaborative attitudes, which in turn predict teacher job satisfaction, with classroom self-efficacy and gender moderating key pathways. Missing data were handled via pairwise deletion, and the constructs were validated using CFA before estimating the structural relations. The results show a significant positive direct effect of collaboration beliefs on collaborative attitudes (β = 0.162, p < 0.001), no significant direct effect of collaboration beliefs on job satisfaction (β = 0.002, p > 0.646), but a significant indirect effect through collaborative attitudes (β = 0.012, p < 0.001) and a significant direct effect of collaborative attitudes on job satisfaction (β = 0.073, p < 0.001). Because the design is cross-sectional and the manuscript does not document the use of PISA teacher sampling weights, causal claims and population-representativeness precision should be interpreted cautiously.
